items.explanation: The drawing is part of a patent application: legal paperwork through which Bell claimed the telephone as his invention. That is what the document directly shows — an inventor securing legal rights. It does not show government funding, and the drawing depicts the device, not a national network, which Bell did not personally construct. Patents were meant to encourage commercialization by protecting inventors, not to block it. The document illustrates the first step of the era's pattern: inventors claimed ideas legally, while organizing capital and building businesses — the step that produced the great fortunes — was largely separate work.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — Bell's telephone (1876) + PD patent drawing, 1876 (stimulus)

option_explanations.A: Nothing in a patent application shows government funding; patents are private legal claims, not grants of public money.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The document is Bell legally claiming his invention — the inventor's step. Building the telephone business was done by organizers and investors, a separate step.
option_explanations.C: The drawing shows the telephone device, not a network, and Bell did not personally construct a nationwide system.
option_explanations.D: Patents did the opposite: by protecting an inventor's claim, they encouraged investors to commercialize new ideas.

options: (A) The federal government funded most of the era's important inventions through direct grants and supervised their commercial development.
(B) Inventors used the patent system to claim legal ownership of their ideas, which entrepreneurs and investors then built into businesses.
(C) Bell personally designed, financed, and constructed the nationwide telephone network depicted in the drawing.
(D) Patent law blocked new inventions from reaching the market by denying inventors any legal protection for their work.

items.explanation: Edison's 1879 bulb made electric light practical, and its economic importance was extending usable hours: factories, stores, and streets could be lit brightly and safely after dark. Gas lamps were replaced gradually over decades, not in a year. Early electric lighting served cities, not isolated farmhouses. Bulbs consumed electricity generated largely by coal-burning stations; they did not end coal demand.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — Edison's light bulb (1879) 'rewired daily life'

option_explanations.A: Adoption took decades; no technology replaced a whole lighting system in one year.
option_explanations.B: Early electric service was an urban phenomenon — power stations served dense city districts.
option_explanations.C: Light bulbs use electricity; the power stations that supplied it burned coal.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Practical electric light extended the business day and rewired daily life.

options: (A) replaced every gas lamp in American cities within a single year of its invention, ending the gas-lighting era almost overnight
(B) was adopted mainly in isolated rural farmhouses, where gas lines could not reach and no other lighting alternative existed
(C) ended the demand for coal entirely, since the new bulbs generated their own electric power without burning any fuel
(D) made electric lighting practical for factories, shops, and streets, extending the hours when business could be done

items.explanation: Menlo Park was a private research laboratory: a team of workers developing inventions as organized, paid work. That was the significant change — invention becoming a business function. It was not a university or a government project. Independent inventors kept working long after 1880; Menlo Park added a new model rather than ending the old one.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — Edison's light bulb (1879) + PD photograph of Menlo Park laboratory, late 1870s (stimulus); organized-R&D interpretation flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: This was a private business laboratory, not a university.
option_explanations.B: No government agency directed or funded this work.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The photograph shows invention organized as team-based, business-funded work.
option_explanations.D: Overstatement: independent inventors continued working for decades afterward.

options: (A) proved that American universities had taken over scientific research from private businesses by the late 1870s
(B) showed that the federal government directed and funded the era's most important technological research programs
(C) turned invention into organized, team-based work funded by business rather than the effort of a lone inventor
(D) meant that independent inventors stopped inventing entirely after 1880, leaving all research to corporations

items.explanation: The engraving literally shows the infrastructure work: crews burying electric lines for a new power station. Electricity could not piggyback on gas pipes; it needed its own system. The work shown is happening in New York City in 1882 — urban first, not small towns first — and it was underway, not delayed for decades.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The image shows the new infrastructure — buried lines for a new power station — being built.
option_explanations.B: The scene is New York City; electrification began in dense urban districts.
option_explanations.C: The workers are laying new electric lines, not reusing gas pipes.
option_explanations.D: The 1882 date shows the work happening, not delayed.

options: (A) It required building an entirely new infrastructure — wires, stations, and equipment — beneath and above city streets.
(B) It was adopted first in small towns, where installation was cheapest and where existing systems were simplest to convert.
(C) It needed no new construction because the electric lines could simply be run through the existing gas pipes.
(D) It was delayed for decades because city governments refused to allow any of the necessary construction work.

items.explanation: Pearl Street was the first central power station: it generated electricity in one place and sold it to customers nearby. That business model — power as a utility service — was as important as the machinery. The dynamo certainly had business significance. Edison's company charged customers; it did not give power away. The station served part of lower Manhattan, not the whole country.

option_explanations.A: The dynamo's whole purpose was commercial: generating power to sell.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Central generation plus paying customers made electricity a utility business.
option_explanations.C: Edison's station was a commercial venture; customers paid for the power.
option_explanations.D: Overstatement: the station served nearby customers in lower Manhattan.

options: (A) a technical one only: the dynamo itself, an impressive machine whose importance was purely mechanical rather than commercial
(B) producing electricity in one central station and selling it to many nearby customers, making power a business
(C) giving electricity away free to the public in order to prove to everyone that electric light was better than gas
(D) powering the entire United States from a single large building located in lower Manhattan

items.explanation: Owning every stage from raw materials to finished product is vertical integration — owning every step from mine to market, as Carnegie did in steel. Horizontal integration means buying out competitors at the same stage, as Rockefeller did with refineries. A trust combines separate companies under one board to limit competition. Collective bargaining is negotiation between a union and an employer.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Vertical / horizontal integration — Controlling every production stage (Carnegie)... owning every step from mine to market

option_explanations.A: Correct. Controlling each production stage — mines, fuel, transport, mills — is vertical integration.
option_explanations.B: Horizontal integration is buying out rival firms at the same stage, not controlling successive stages.
option_explanations.C: A trust combines competing companies under one board; it does not mean owning the supply chain.
option_explanations.D: Collective bargaining is union-employer negotiation, not a business-ownership strategy.

options: (A) vertical integration
(B) horizontal integration
(C) a trust
(D) collective bargaining

items.explanation: Before Bessemer, steel was too expensive for large-scale use; the process made it cheap, which is why rails, bridges, and skyscrapers became economical. Iron had been made for thousands of years — Bessemer made steel affordable. Steel mills still employed thousands of workers. Wood remained a common building material.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Bessemer process — Cheap steelmaking method adopted in the 1870s; made skyscrapers, rails, and bridges economical

option_explanations.A: Iron predates the Bessemer process by millennia; the breakthrough was cheap steel.
option_explanations.B: Steel mills remained labor-intensive workplaces.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Cheap steel is what made rails, bridges, and skyscrapers economical.
option_explanations.D: Overstatement: wood stayed cheap and widely used in construction.

options: (A) was the first method ever devised for making iron in any form throughout history
(B) allowed factories to operate entirely without employing any workers at all
(C) made steel cheap enough to use for rails, bridges, and tall buildings
(D) ended the use of wood in all American construction projects permanently

items.explanation: The Bessemer process of the 1870s lowered steel's cost, which made a steel bridge across the Mississippi affordable; building such projects then expanded the market for steel producers — a feedback loop between technology and business. The causation in the first option is reversed: the process came first. The bridge carried rail and road traffic, not primarily telegraph wires. The Eads Bridge was a private enterprise, not proof that private firms couldn't build big things.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Bessemer process (1870s; made bridges economical) + §The story — Bessemer process made steel cheap in the 1870s

option_explanations.A: Reversed causation: the Bessemer process (1870s) made the steel bridge possible, not the other way around.
option_explanations.B: The bridge carried railroads and roadways; telegraph wires were incidental.
option_explanations.C: The bridge was privately built — evidence that private firms could finance giant projects.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Cheap steel enabled the bridge, and the bridge (and others like it) fed demand back to steelmakers.

options: (A) Bridge building created the commercial demand that directly caused the invention of the Bessemer process.
(B) Steel bridges were built mainly to carry telegraph wires across wide rivers.
(C) The bridge proved that private companies could no longer afford large-scale construction projects on their own.
(D) Cheaper steel made giant projects possible, and those projects then created still more demand for steel.

items.explanation: A steel bridge on this scale required cheap steel, which only existed after the Bessemer process was adopted in the 1870s. The steel industry remained private — no nationalization occurred. Engineers had built many bridges before; the barrier was the cost of steel, not know-how. Wood stayed cheap and widely used.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Bessemer process — adopted in the 1870s; made... bridges economical

option_explanations.A: The steel industry stayed in private hands throughout the Gilded Age.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Only cheap Bessemer steel made a steel bridge of this size affordable.
option_explanations.C: Engineers had built many bridges; the new factor was affordable steel.
option_explanations.D: Wood remained cheap and common as a building material.

options: (A) the federal government had nationalized the steel industry in the 1870s
(B) the Bessemer process had made steel affordable in the 1870s
(C) American engineers had never built a bridge of any kind before
(D) wood had become too expensive for any construction work

items.explanation: The image is a criticism of concentrated corporate power: Vanderbilt bestrides the country like a giant, suggesting the railroads had grown beyond democratic restraint. It is caricature, not a literal claim that one man laid all the track. The tentacles show reach and strength, not weakness. No railroad breakup had occurred in 1879.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The giant figure expresses the cartoonist's criticism: railroad corporations had become dangerously powerful.
option_explanations.B: Caricature is not literal reporting; the point is power, not track-laying.
option_explanations.C: The spreading tentacles show overwhelming reach — the opposite of weakness.
option_explanations.D: No such breakup occurred in 1879; the railroads were at the height of their power.

options: (A) railroad corporations had grown powerful enough to dominate the economy and threaten democratic control

(D) the government had already broken up all the railroad companies into small local lines

option_explanations.B: Railroads stayed private; Populist demands for public ownership failed.

option_explanations.D: Factory production grew with rail access; it did not decline.

options: (A) the end of farming, as railroads replaced agriculture as the nation's principal economic base
(B) government ownership of all American industry, with Washington directly managing the operations of every firm

items.explanation: The cartoon shows the artist's view that corporate interests dominated the Senate — evidence of how big business's political power was perceived. It shows lobbyists present and powerful, not senators refusing to meet them, and not corporations ignoring Washington. But a cartoon expresses an opinion; it cannot prove that any individual senator took a bribe — that overreads what this kind of source can establish.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — trusts, holding companies... built empires + §What the exam tests — government's pro-business stance + PD cartoon (Puck, 1889)

option_explanations.A: The image shows lobbyists looming over willing senators — the opposite of refusal.
option_explanations.B: A cartoon shows the artist's opinion; it cannot prove individual acts of bribery.
option_explanations.C: The cartoon's whole point is that corporations cared deeply about federal policy.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The cartoon is evidence that corporate influence over government was widely perceived.

options: (A) Senators of the era refused to meet with any business leaders or lobbyists.

items.explanation: Buying competitors at the same stage of production (refining) is horizontal integration — Rockefeller's method. Vertical integration means controlling successive stages from raw material to finished product, as Carnegie did in steel. A labor union organizes workers. The Homestead Act gave western land to settlers.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Buying up rival refineries — competitors at the same stage — is horizontal integration.
option_explanations.B: Vertical integration is controlling successive stages from raw material to product; that was Carnegie's steel method.
option_explanations.C: A labor union organizes workers, not companies.
option_explanations.D: The Homestead Act granted western land to settlers; it has nothing to do with oil refining.

options: (A) horizontal integration — combining with competitors at the same stage

items.explanation: Trusts existed to kill competition and fix prices — Standard Oil is the textbook example. They did the opposite of increasing competition. They were combinations of companies, not worker organizations. The Sherman Act outlawed restraints of trade but was weakly enforced against big business at first, so trusts thrived after 1890.
items.fact_source: u6.md §Key terms — Trust — Combination of companies under one board to kill competition and fix prices (e.g., Standard Oil) + Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) — weakly enforced against big business at first

option_explanations.B: Correct. Trusts combined firms to limit competition and control prices.
option_explanations.C: Trusts combined companies; unions organized workers.
option_explanations.D: The Sherman Act was weakly enforced at first, so trusts continued to thrive after 1890.

options: (A) Trusts were designed to increase competition among small businesses by breaking up monopolies.

(D) Trusts were quickly destroyed by the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 after its passage.

It was not trying to destroy corporations. Trusts flourished after 1890; they had not disappeared. Courts of the era were hostile to unions, not their defenders.

Paperwork grew with corporate size; the phone did not eliminate records.

items.explanation: The ICC was the first federal railroad regulation, created after farmers — squeezed between falling crop prices and freight rates they couldn't control — won state rate laws and demanded federal action. It regulated railroads; it did not free them from oversight. Standard Oil's breakup came decades later and concerned oil, not railroads. It addressed rates, not labor rights.

option_explanations.B: Standard Oil was broken up decades later, in 1911 — and it was an oil company, not a railroad.
option_explanations.C: The ICC regulated railroad rates, not labor rights.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The ICC was the first federal railroad regulation, answering farmers' grievances over rates.

Defenders did not claim wages rose for all; industry stayed private, not government-owned; and nobody disputes that the economy grew enormously.

option_explanations.D: Both sides agreed the economy grew enormously; they disagreed about who benefited.

items.stem: As large corporations grew in the Gilded Age, they employed growing numbers of clerks, bookkeepers, managers, salesmen, and stenographers. These white-collar jobs existed mainly because
options: (A) factory owners needed more manual laborers to operate the new machinery
(B) large corporations needed office workers to handle paperwork, accounts, and coordination across their operations
(C) the federal government hired millions of new civil servants under civil service reform, creating a government workforce larger than the private office workforce
(D) immigrants refused to do factory work, so employers created office jobs instead
items.explanation: Corporate growth created the need for office staff: big firms had paperwork, accounts, and far-flung operations to manage, and clerks, bookkeepers, managers, salesmen, and stenographers did that non-manual work.

option_explanations.A: These were office jobs, not manual-labor jobs; factory hands operated the machinery.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Expanding corporations needed armies of office workers to manage their paperwork and coordination.
option_explanations.C: Civil service reform affected only a small federal workforce, not millions of workers.
option_explanations.D: Immigrants filled factory jobs in large numbers; office jobs were not created as a substitute for factory labor.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — corporations needed armies of clerks, bookkeepers, managers, salesmen, stenographers

stimulus.image_caption: Remington Standard Typewriter, 1890.

items.stem: The spread of machines like the 1890 typewriter shown here helped change the makeup of the American office workforce because
options: (A) typewriters eliminated the need for office workers entirely
(B) only men were permitted to operate typewriters in American offices
(C) employers hired large numbers of women as typists and stenographers as typewriters and telephones multiplied
(D) typewriters required every manager to write out all correspondence by hand
items.explanation: The typewriter and the telephone created new clerical jobs, and employers filled those jobs — typist, stenographer, telephone operator — largely with women, bringing women into the office workforce in large numbers.

option_explanations.A: Typewriters created office jobs rather than eliminating them.
option_explanations.B: Women, not men alone, became the main operators of these machines in offices.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The new office machines opened clerical work to large numbers of women.
option_explanations.D: Managers dictated or assigned correspondence; the new machines did not return managers to handwriting.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — women entered the office workforce in large numbers as typewriters and telephones multiplied

stimulus.image_caption: Newspaper advertisement for H. Leh & Company department store, Allentown, Pennsylvania, 1890.

items.stem: This 1890 newspaper advertisement for a department store illustrates the beginnings of a consumer culture in the Gilded Age. Department stores such as Macy's, Marshall Field's, and Wanamaker's changed American shopping by
options: (A) offering fixed prices, advertised goods, and brand names, and making shopping itself a leisure activity
(B) selling only luxury goods that ordinary middle-class families could not afford, serving a tiny elite of wealthy shoppers
(C) requiring every customer to haggle over the price of each item
(D) conducting all of their business through mail-order catalogs
items.explanation: Department stores built consumer culture on fixed prices, advertising, and brand names, and they made shopping a leisure pastime — the ad itself, listing goods with set prices, is an example of the new advertising.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Fixed prices, advertising, brand names, and shopping as leisure were the department store's innovations.
option_explanations.B: Department stores served the broad middle class, not only the wealthy.
option_explanations.C: Fixed prices replaced haggling; that was one of the stores' defining changes.
option_explanations.D: Mail-order catalogs were the business of Montgomery Ward and Sears, not of the big city department stores.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — department stores (Macy's, Marshall Field's, Wanamaker's); fixed prices, advertising, brand names, shopping as leisure

stimulus.image_caption: Floor plan of the first floor of Macy's Department Store, New York, as built 1901–1902.

items.stem: The image is the 1902 floor plan of the first floor of Macy's department store in New York. As a piece of historical evidence, this plan best supports which conclusion?
options: (A) Most Americans did their shopping in department stores by 1902
(B) department stores caused the decline of small-town general stores, since every rural family abandoned local shops to travel to the city
(C) Macy's sold a larger volume of goods than any other American retailer
(D) department stores were large, carefully organized retail enterprises built to display a wide variety of goods under one roof
items.explanation: The plan shows a single floor divided into many departments for different goods — direct evidence of the department store's scale and deliberate organization. It says nothing about national shopping habits, causes of other stores' decline, or sales rankings.

option_explanations.A: One store's floor plan cannot show where most Americans shopped.
option_explanations.B: The plan shows one building's layout; it cannot establish what caused another kind of store to decline.
option_explanations.C: A floor plan shows layout, not sales volume or rank among retailers.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The plan documents a large retail space deliberately divided into departments for displaying many kinds of goods.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — department stores (Macy's, Marshall Field's, Wanamaker's); beginnings of consumer culture

stimulus.image_caption: Stereoscopic view of the Montgomery Ward & Co. establishment, Chicago.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 19th-century stereoscopic view, Robert N. Dennis collection; LicenseShortName Public domain

items.stem: The stereoscopic view shows the Montgomery Ward & Co. building in Chicago. Firms like Montgomery Ward and Sears built their business on mail-order catalogs, which mattered most to
options: (A) wealthy shoppers who lived near big-city department stores and could visit their marble halls in person whenever they wished
(B) customers in small towns and rural areas far from city stores, who could order brand-name goods by mail
(C) factory owners purchasing heavy industrial machinery
(D) recent immigrants arriving at Ellis Island
items.explanation: Mail-order catalogs extended the new consumer culture beyond the cities: customers far from department stores could order advertised, brand-name goods by mail.

option_explanations.A: City shoppers could visit department stores in person; catalogs served those who could not.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Catalogs brought department-store-style goods to small-town and rural customers.
option_explanations.C: Catalogs sold household and consumer goods, not industrial machinery.
option_explanations.D: Newly arrived immigrants were not the catalogs' main market.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — mail-order catalogs (Montgomery Ward, Sears) built the beginnings of a consumer culture

stimulus.image_caption: Electric streetcars on Canal Street, 1907 postcard view.

items.stem: The 1907 view shows electric streetcars on Canal Street. Electric streetcars helped create 'streetcar suburbs' because they
options: (A) allowed families to live farther from their workplaces, separating home from work and making suburban homeownership possible for the middle class
(B) were the first form of public transportation ever used in American cities
(C) carried shoppers to downtown department stores and nowhere else
(D) replaced railroads as the main carriers of freight
items.explanation: Electric streetcars made it practical to commute from farther out, so middle-class families could move to early suburbs — separating the home from the workplace and making homeownership the class's defining aspiration.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Streetcars extended the commuting range, enabling suburbs and middle-class homeownership.
option_explanations.B: Horse-drawn streetcars and omnibuses came before electric ones.
option_explanations.C: Streetcars served commuters across the city, not only shoppers.
option_explanations.D: Streetcars carried passengers within cities; railroads remained the freight carriers.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — electric streetcars let families move to early suburbs (streetcar suburbs), separating home from workplace; homeownership the class's defining aspiration

items.stem: The Gilded Age middle class sent more of its children to high school than any earlier generation and enjoyed more leisure time. Those changes help explain why middle-class Americans became
options: (A) the main source of recruits for factory labor
(B) opponents of every form of government regulation, demanding that business and city life be left entirely free of public control
(C) the audience for the era's reform energy — women's clubs, temperance unions, and the readers of the muckrakers
(D) supporters of a mass return to farm life
items.explanation: More schooling and more leisure gave the middle class the time, literacy, and inclination to fill the era's reform audiences — the clubs, temperance unions, and muckraking magazines.

option_explanations.A: Factory labor drew on immigrants and the working class, not the schooled middle class.
option_explanations.B: The middle class would soon demand regulation — pure food, clean cities, honest government.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Schooling and leisure made the middle class the audience for reform energy.
option_explanations.D: The middle class was moving to streetcar suburbs, not back to farms.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — high schools expanded rapidly; more leisure; audiences for reform energy: women's clubs, temperance unions, readers of the muckrakers

items.stem: The review calls the Gilded Age middle class 'Progressivism's foot soldiers': the clerks and professionals who, in the 1900s, demanded pure food, clean cities, and honest government. This description makes its strongest point about
options: (A) the platform of the Populist Party in the 1890s
(B) the reasons industrial workers joined labor unions to fight for higher wages, shorter hours, and safer conditions in factories and mines
(C) the causes of the Panic of 1893
(D) how a class created by industrialization carried its expectations into the reform politics of the Progressive Era
items.explanation: The point connects the Gilded Age to what followed: the middle class industrialization created became, in the 1900s, the constituency demanding pure food, clean cities, and honest government.

option_explanations.A: Populism was a farmers' movement of the 1890s, not the middle-class reformers of the 1900s.
option_explanations.B: Union members were industrial workers; the 'foot soldiers' described here are clerks and professionals.
option_explanations.C: The Panic of 1893 was an economic depression, unrelated to this claim about reform politics.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The description links the middle class's origins in industrialization to its later reform role.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — this class became Progressivism's foot soldiers: demanded pure food, clean cities, honest government in the 1900s

items.stem: "The middle class was industrialization's most durable political product — it bought the system's promises, then turned around and tried to fix the system's abuses." This claim is best judged as
options: (A) false, because the middle class took no part in reform movements
(B) a reasonable judgment: the middle class embraced the new economy's goods, then supplied many Progressive Era reformers
(C) false, because industrialization created no middle class at all
(D) exaggerated, because only factory workers ever demanded reforms, while the middle class stayed home and ignored public life entirely
items.explanation: The claim fits the evidence: the middle class bought department-store goods and new products, then its clerks and professionals filled the Progressive Era's reform campaigns for pure food, clean cities, and honest government.

option_explanations.A: The middle class filled women's clubs, temperance unions, and the muckrakers' readership.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The claim accurately describes a class that embraced the new economy and then tried to reform it.
option_explanations.C: Industrialization created a large new white-collar middle class.
option_explanations.D: Factory workers organized unions; the reformers described here were middle-class clerks and professionals.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — 'The middle class was industrialization's most durable political product — it bought the system's promises, then turned around and tried to fix the system's abuses.'

items.stem: Unlike the factory workers of the Gilded Age, the new white-collar middle class
options: (A) earned salaries for non-manual work, though their incomes still rose and fell with the economy
(B) owned the corporations that employed them
(C) was untouched by economic depressions
(D) performed manual labor in mills, mines, and factories
items.explanation: White-collar workers lived by salaries rather than wages for manual labor, but those salaries still depended on the economy's ups and downs — they were not owners and not insulated from hard times.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Salaried, non-manual work defined the class, without freeing it from economic cycles.
option_explanations.B: Corporations were owned by investors and shareholders, not by their clerks.
option_explanations.C: Their salaries depended on the economy, so depressions affected them too.
option_explanations.D: Manual labor in mills, mines, and factories was the working class's lot, not the white-collar middle class's.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — white-collar workers whose salaries depended on the economy but whose lives no longer involved manual labor

items.stem: A historian claims that department stores turned shopping into a leisure activity for the middle class. Which of the following would be the strongest evidence for that claim?
options: (A) Department stores were located in large cities
(B) Factory wages rose during the 1880s
(C) stores advertised heavily, displayed goods attractively, and drew customers who came to browse as a pastime
(D) most Americans in 1890 still grew much of their own food, canned their own vegetables, and sewed their own clothes at home
items.explanation: Advertising, attractive display, and customers browsing for pleasure are direct evidence that shopping had become a leisure activity, not just a chore.

option_explanations.A: Location alone says nothing about whether shopping was leisure.
option_explanations.B: Rising wages do not show how people experienced shopping.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Heavy advertising, appealing displays, and browsing customers directly support the leisure claim.
option_explanations.D: What most Americans grew is irrelevant to how department-store shoppers behaved.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — advertising, brand names, shopping as leisure

stimulus.image_caption: The Marshall Field wholesale warehouse, Chicago, which supplied the company's department store.

items.stem: The photograph shows the Marshall Field wholesale warehouse in Chicago, which supplied the company's famous department store. The building's large scale best illustrates
options: (A) the poverty of Chicago's working class
(B) the decline of American manufacturing
(C) the federal government's management of retail trade, which set national rules for how stores bought and sold goods
(D) how large retail firms organized the purchase, storage, and distribution of goods on an industrial scale
items.explanation: A warehouse of this size existed to buy, store, and distribute enormous quantities of goods — retail organized on the same large scale as the era's factories and railroads.

option_explanations.A: The photograph shows a commercial building, not workers' living conditions.
option_explanations.B: The building served a thriving retail business; it shows no manufacturing decline.
option_explanations.C: The warehouse was a private firm's operation, not a government project.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The scale of the building reflects industrial-scale organization of retail.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — department stores (Macy's, Marshall Field's, Wanamaker's)

items.stem: Before department stores, shoppers in small shops usually haggled over prices. The department stores' system of fixed, advertised prices mattered because it
options: (A) raised the prices ordinary consumers had to pay
(B) made shopping predictable and impersonal, suited to a mass market of strangers
(C) was required by a federal law regulating retail trade, which fixed the prices merchants could charge
(D) was used only by mail-order catalogs, not by city stores
items.explanation: Fixed prices let strangers shop without personal bargaining — the predictable, impersonal transaction a mass market required.

option_explanations.A: Fixed prices brought predictability, not necessarily higher prices.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Fixed prices suited a mass market of strangers, replacing personal haggling.
option_explanations.C: No federal law required fixed prices; it was a business practice.
option_explanations.D: Department stores used fixed prices in their city stores; catalogs used them in print.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — fixed prices, advertising, brand names

items.stem: Gilded Age middle-class Americans eagerly bought department-store goods and labor-saving products, yet many of the same people later joined campaigns for pure food laws and honest government. This pattern best illustrates
options: (A) continuity and change: the middle class kept its faith in the economy's benefits while pushing to correct its harms
(B) a complete rejection of industrial capitalism by the middle class
(C) the triumph of laissez-faire ideas over all reform efforts, which ended every campaign for pure food, clean cities, and honest government
(D) the decline of consumer culture in the early 1900s
items.explanation: The middle class did not abandon the industrial economy — it kept buying its goods — but it also demanded reforms to its abuses, showing continuity of faith in the system alongside change in political demands.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The pattern shows continued embrace of the economy's benefits plus new demands to fix its harms.
option_explanations.B: Eager buying of the system's goods contradicts any claim of complete rejection.
option_explanations.C: Demands for pure food laws and honest government contradict laissez-faire triumph.
option_explanations.D: Consumer culture kept growing; it did not decline.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — 'it bought the system's promises, then turned around and tried to fix the system's abuses'

items.stem: Women entered the office workforce in large numbers during the Gilded Age. The typewriter and the telephone contributed to this change mainly by
options: (A) making office work too dangerous for men to perform
(B) requiring college degrees that only women held at the time, shutting men out of the new office jobs entirely
(C) eliminating clerical jobs from American offices
(D) creating new clerical jobs — typist, stenographer, telephone operator — largely filled by women
items.explanation: The new machines created new categories of clerical work, and as typewriters and telephones multiplied, employers hired large numbers of women to do it.

option_explanations.A: Office work was not dangerous; danger does not explain the change.
option_explanations.B: These jobs did not require college degrees, and women did not uniquely hold degrees.
option_explanations.C: The machines added clerical jobs rather than eliminating them.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The new machines generated clerical jobs that brought women into offices in large numbers.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — women entered the office workforce in large numbers as typewriters and telephones multiplied

items.stem: Compared with the small general store, the department store represented
options: (A) a return to barter and trade in kind
(B) a smaller and narrower selection of goods
(C) retail organized on the same large scale as the era's factories and railroads
(D) a rejection of advertising and brand names
items.explanation: Like the era's big factories and railroad systems, the department store concentrated activity on a large scale — many departments, many goods, many customers under one roof — where the general store had been small and personal.

option_explanations.A: Department stores used money prices, not barter.
option_explanations.B: Department stores offered a far wider selection than general stores.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The department store applied large-scale organization to retail.
option_explanations.D: Advertising and brand names were central to the department store's methods.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — department stores (Macy's, Marshall Field's, Wanamaker's); advertising, brand names

items.stem: A historian finds an 1890 department-store newspaper advertisement listing dozens of goods with fixed prices. The advertisement is strong evidence of what the store wanted customers to see, but by itself it cannot show
options: (A) the store's advertising strategy
(B) whether most families could afford the goods, or how the store's clerks worked
(C) the kinds of goods a department store sold
(D) that fixed prices were part of the store's appeal, drawing customers who disliked haggling
items.explanation: An ad documents the store's pitch — goods, prices, image — but it cannot tell us about customers' actual purchasing power or about the working conditions of the clerks behind the counters.

option_explanations.A: The ad itself is the advertising strategy, so it documents that directly.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Affordability for families and clerks' working conditions lie outside what an ad can show.
option_explanations.C: The listed goods directly show what the store sold.
option_explanations.D: Printed fixed prices directly show that fixed prices were part of the appeal.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — fixed prices, advertising; white-collar clerks

items.stem: Homeownership became a defining aspiration of the Gilded Age middle class. The growth of streetcar suburbs made that aspiration achievable for more families because
options: (A) the federal government granted free suburban land to office workers through a special suburban homestead program for clerks
(B) streetcar companies carried all passengers free of charge
(C) factories relocated into the new suburbs
(D) affordable land farther from city centers became practical to reach each day by electric streetcar
items.explanation: Streetcars extended the daily commute, so families could buy cheaper land beyond the city center and still reach their workplaces — the mechanism behind the streetcar suburb.

option_explanations.A: Free federal land grants went to rural settlers, not suburban office workers.
option_explanations.B: Streetcars charged fares; they were not free.
option_explanations.C: Suburbs were residential; factories stayed in industrial districts.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The streetcar made distant, affordable land a practical home for commuters.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — streetcar suburbs; homeownership the class's defining aspiration

stimulus.text: 'There was a South of slavery and secession — that South is dead. There is a South of union and freedom — that South, thank God, is living, breathing, growing every hour.' (Henry W. Grady, 'The New South' speech, December 1886)

items.stem: Grady, an Atlanta newspaper editor, delivered this address to an audience of New York businessmen. The passage and its setting together show that the 'New South' creed was
options: (A) a military plan to reoccupy the Southern states
(B) a defense of slavery and secession
(C) a pitch for reconciliation through commerce, inviting Northern investors to industrialize the South
(D) a demand for Southern political independence from the United States, withdrawing the Southern states from the Union
items.explanation: Grady preached reconciliation through commerce to the very men whose capital he wanted: the creed promised that railroads, mills, and Northern investment would industrialize the South and close the wealth gap with the North.

option_explanations.A: The speech was an economic appeal, not a military plan.
option_explanations.B: Grady declares the South of slavery 'dead'; he does not defend it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The address courted Northern businessmen with a promise of profitable reconciliation.
option_explanations.D: Grady celebrates 'a South of union,' not independence.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — Grady's 1886 address to New York businessmen preached reconciliation through commerce

stimulus.text: 'The old South rested everything on slavery and agriculture, unconscious that these could neither give nor maintain healthy growth. The new South presents a perfect democracy... a hundred farms for every plantation, fifty homes for every palace; and a diversified industry that meets the complex needs of this complex age.' (Henry W. Grady, 'The New South' speech, December 1886)

items.stem: In this passage, Grady promises that the New South will differ from the Old South by
options: (A) replacing plantation agriculture with small farms and diversified industry
(B) restoring slavery under a different name
(C) rejecting industry and returning to plantation agriculture
(D) seeking political separation from the United States
items.explanation: Grady's contrast is explicit: the old South rested on slavery and plantation agriculture; the new South would have many small farms and diversified industry.

option_explanations.A: Correct. 'A hundred farms for every plantation' and 'diversified industry' state the promise directly.
option_explanations.B: Grady presents the new South as a break from slavery, not its restoration.
option_explanations.C: Diversified industry is central to the passage; Grady does not reject industry.
option_explanations.D: The speech celebrates union, not separation.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — creed promised railroads, mills, Northern capital would industrialize the region and close the wealth gap with the North

stimulus.image_caption: Henry W. Grady, Atlanta newspaper editor and spokesman for the 'New South' creed.

items.stem: A historian wants to use Grady's 1886 'New South' speech to describe the actual economic conditions of Southern farmers in the 1880s. The most serious limitation of the speech for that purpose is that
options: (A) Grady was a Northerner with no knowledge of the South
(B) the speech was never published or widely read
(C) no Southerners ever heard the speech or read about the New South campaign in their newspapers
(D) Grady was a booster addressing Northern investors
items.explanation: A booster speaking to investors describes an opportunity, not a reality. Most Southerners in the 1880s were poor farmers trapped by sharecropping and debt — the opposite of the prosperous industrial South Grady advertised.

option_explanations.A: Grady was an Atlanta editor, a Southerner promoting his region.
option_explanations.B: The speech was famous and widely reprinted.
option_explanations.C: Southern newspapers and audiences followed Grady's campaign closely.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The speech's purpose — attracting Northern capital — limits its value as evidence of farmers' actual conditions.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — Grady's 1886 address to New York businessmen; reality fell far short: most Southerners stayed poor farmers trapped by sharecropping and the crop-lien system

items.stem: Critics of the crop-lien system called it 'wage slavery in a new form.' The comparison was meant to argue that
options: (A) sharecroppers earned higher wages than Northern factory workers and accumulated savings faster than any other laborers
(B) like slavery, the system used debt and legal control to bind laborers to the land
(C) the federal government had reintroduced slavery in the South
(D) Southern landowners paid their tenants fair and honest wages
items.explanation: The critics' point was about coercion's continuity: landless tenants bought supplies on credit at inflated prices and paid in cotton, ending each year deeper in debt — bound to the land by economics and law rather than by legal ownership.

option_explanations.A: Sharecroppers were among the poorest laborers in the country, not high earners.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The phrase targeted the system's coercive control over labor, echoing slavery.
option_explanations.C: Slavery remained abolished; the criticism was about economic coercion, not legal reintroduction.
option_explanations.D: The system trapped tenants in debt; fair wages were not its feature.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — crop-lien system: landless tenants bought supplies on credit at inflated prices, paid in cotton, ended each year deeper in debt; critics called it 'wage slavery in a new form'

stimulus.image_caption: 'The new South — the triumph of free labor,' chromolithograph by Joseph Keppler for Puck magazine, 1895.

items.stem: This 1895 Puck cartoon by Joseph Keppler celebrates the New South as 'the triumph of free labor.' Judged against the historical evidence, the cartoon's claim is best described as
options: (A) accurate, because Southern industry had eliminated rural poverty
(B) proven by the success of Grady's promises
(C) overstated: most Southerners remained poor farmers trapped by debt, and the region stayed the nation's poorest
(D) wrong, because Northern capital never invested in the South, leaving the region without any railroads, mills, or factories at all
items.explanation: The cartoon celebrates the creed, but the evidence shows the creed's limits: industrialization was partial, most Southerners stayed poor farmers in debt, and the South remained the nation's poorest region.

option_explanations.A: Rural poverty persisted; industry did not eliminate it.
option_explanations.B: Grady's promises were only partly fulfilled — the reality fell far short.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The evidence supports partial change, not the cartoon's triumphant claim.
option_explanations.D: Northern capital did invest in the South — that was part of the problem's shape, since the capital mostly came from the North.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — reality fell far short of the promise; region stayed the nation's poorest

stimulus.text: 'All must work under my direction.... No sharecropper is to work off the plantation when there is any work for them to do for me. Nothing can be sold from their crops until my rent is all paid, and all amounts they owe me are paid in full.' (Sharecropping contract, Grimes family papers, North Carolina, 1882)

items.stem: This contract shows that the sharecropping system gave landowners
options: (A) close control over tenants' labor and over when and how their crops could be sold
(B) no role in the daily work of the farm
(C) an obligation to pay their tenants fixed yearly wages
(D) a duty to cancel their tenants' debts at the end of each year
items.explanation: The contract's terms are explicit: tenants work under the landowner's direction, cannot work elsewhere, and cannot sell anything until rent and debts are paid in full.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The quoted terms give the landowner direction of labor and control of crop sales.
option_explanations.B: 'All must work under my direction' gives the landowner a direct daily role.
option_explanations.C: Sharecroppers were paid in a share of the crop, not fixed wages.
option_explanations.D: The contract protects the landowner's debts — 'until... all amounts they owe me are paid in full' — not the tenant.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — sharecropping and the crop-lien system trapped poor farmers

stimulus.text: 'The sale of every sharecropper's part of the cotton to be made by me when and where I choose to sell, and after taking all they owe me.' (Sharecropping contract, Grimes family papers, North Carolina, 1882)

items.stem: Under this contract, the sharecropper could neither sell his own cotton nor choose when to sell it. This arrangement most directly continued which feature of the slavery-era plantation economy?
options: (A) The use of overseers to discipline field workers
(B) The legal ownership of human beings as property
(C) The growth of diversified manufacturing
(D) The landowner's control over the crop and over the labor that produced it
items.explanation: What continued was the plantation's core power relationship: the landowner controlled the crop and the labor, even though the legal form had changed from ownership of people to control through debt and contract.

option_explanations.A: The contract mentions direction of work, not overseers or discipline.
option_explanations.B: Legal ownership of people ended with emancipation; the contract controls labor by other means.
option_explanations.C: The contract concerns cotton farming, not manufacturing.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Control of crop and labor is the continuous feature.

stimulus.image_caption: First page of a sharecropping contract, De Soto County, Mississippi, 1867.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Document dated 1867; pre-1930, LicenseShortName Public domain

items.stem: The image shows the first page of an 1867 sharecropping contract from De Soto County, Mississippi. As a primary source, this document is most valuable for showing
options: (A) the wealth Southern planters enjoyed after the Civil War, documenting how quickly planters rebuilt their antebellum fortunes
(B) the specific legal terms — shares, duties, and restrictions — that bound tenants to landowners after emancipation
(C) the opinions Northern investors held about the Southern economy
(D) the text of Mississippi's 1890 constitution
items.explanation: A contract's value as evidence is in its terms: the shares, duties, and restrictions it imposed — the legal machinery that bound tenants to landowners in freedom's first years.

option_explanations.A: A contract's terms show obligations, not the planter's wealth.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The document's terms are its historical evidence.
option_explanations.C: The contract records a Mississippi agreement, not Northern investors' opinions.
option_explanations.D: This is an 1867 labor contract, not the 1890 constitution.

stimulus.image_caption: Bird's-eye view of the business section, Birmingham, Alabama, between 1890 and 1910.

items.stem: The New South's boosters did build real industry — iron and steel in Birmingham, textile mills across the Carolina Piedmont, tobacco factories in North Carolina — and Southern cities grew fast. This bird's-eye view of Birmingham's business district best illustrates
options: (A) the genuine but limited industrial growth the New South creed could point to
(B) the complete transformation of the Southern economy
(C) the absence of Northern investment in the South
(D) the end of poverty in the Southern states
items.explanation: Birmingham's growth was real — the creed's supporters could point to it honestly — but it was limited: most Southerners stayed poor farmers, and the region remained the nation's poorest.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The image shows real urban industrial growth, which was genuine yet limited.
option_explanations.B: 'Complete transformation' overstates what the evidence supports.
option_explanations.C: The capital behind this growth came mostly from the North.
option_explanations.D: Southern poverty persisted; the region stayed the nation's poorest.

stimulus.image_caption: Child sweepers in a cotton mill, North Carolina, photographed by Lewis Hine, 1908.

items.stem: Southern mill villages were often company towns, and mill wages ran below Northern levels. This photograph of child sweepers in a North Carolina cotton mill best supports which conclusion about the New South's industrial promise?
options: (A) Southern mills hired only adult men
(B) Northern capital refused to invest in Southern mills, forcing Southerners to build every mill entirely with local savings
(C) mill work in the South was safe and well paid
(D) industrial jobs did not lift most Southern workers out of poverty, as low-wage labor remained common
items.explanation: The photograph shows children doing low-wage mill work — evidence that the New South's industry rested on cheap labor and did not deliver the prosperity the creed promised to most Southerners.

option_explanations.A: The photograph itself shows children, not only adult men, at work.
option_explanations.B: Northern capital did invest in Southern mills; the capital mostly came from the North.
option_explanations.C: Child sweepers indicate low-wage, demanding work, not safe, well-paid jobs.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The image documents the low-wage labor on which Southern industry depended.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — mill villages often company towns with wages below Northern levels; capital mostly from the North

stimulus.image_caption: A young spinner at the Vivian Cotton Mills, Cherryville, North Carolina, photographed by Lewis Hine, 1908.

items.stem: This 1908 photograph shows a young spinner at the Vivian Cotton Mills in Cherryville, North Carolina. The photograph is strong evidence that mills employed young workers at demanding jobs, but by itself it cannot establish
options: (A) that the girl in the photograph worked in a cotton mill
(B) how typical her situation was across Southern mills, or what wages mill villages paid
(C) that the photograph was taken in North Carolina
(D) that cotton mills operated in the Southern states, since the image shows one mill running its machinery
items.explanation: One photograph documents one worker's situation. It cannot show how widespread that situation was, or what mill villages paid — those claims need broader evidence such as payroll records or census data.

option_explanations.A: The image directly shows a young worker at mill machinery.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Typicality and wage levels are beyond what a single photograph can establish.
option_explanations.C: The caption and source identify the location as Cherryville, North Carolina.
option_explanations.D: The photograph itself shows a Southern cotton mill in operation.

stimulus.text: 'A uniform poll tax of two dollars, to be used in aid of the common schools, and for no other purpose, is hereby imposed on every male inhabitant of this State between the ages of twenty-one and sixty years...' (Constitution of Mississippi, adopted November 1, 1890, Art. 12, Sec. 243)

items.stem: Beginning in the 1890s, new state constitutions across the South added requirements like this poll tax. The purpose of such requirements was to
options: (A) fund the public schools fairly and honestly
(B) encourage Black men to register and vote
(C) strip Black men of the vote by making registration costly and difficult
(D) carry out the requirements of the Fifteenth Amendment
items.explanation: Poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses were the legal machinery of disfranchisement: they stripped Black men of the vote while the Fifteenth Amendment was evaded rather than obeyed.

option_explanations.A: School funding was the stated justification; disfranchisement was the purpose.
option_explanations.B: The requirements were designed to exclude Black voters, not encourage them.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Costly, difficult registration requirements were tools for stripping Black men of the vote.
option_explanations.D: The Fifteenth Amendment forbids denying the vote by race; these constitutions evaded it.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — starting with Mississippi's 1890 constitution: poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses stripped Black men of the vote

stimulus.text: 'Every elector shall, in addition to the foregoing qualifications, be able to read any section of the constitution of this State; or he shall be able to understand the same when read to him, or give a reasonable interpretation thereof.' (Mississippi Constitution, 1890, Art. 12, Sec. 244)

items.stem: The 'understanding clause' in this section let local registrars judge whether a voter 'understood' the constitution. The clause worked as a tool of disfranchisement mainly because
options: (A) it gave white registrars discretion to pass white applicants and fail Black applicants
(B) it applied only to immigrants from southern and eastern Europe, leaving native-born voters entirely exempt
(C) the Supreme Court struck it down within a year of its adoption
(D) it required every voter to own property
items.explanation: The clause's power was its vagueness: registrars could accept any interpretation from a white applicant and reject any from a Black applicant, making discrimination the mechanism of disfranchisement.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Registrar discretion was the tool that turned a literacy test into racial exclusion.
option_explanations.B: The clause applied to all voters; its targets were Black Southerners.
option_explanations.C: The constitutions survived; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) protected them.
option_explanations.D: The section concerns reading and understanding, not property ownership.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — Mississippi's 1890 constitution: literacy tests stripped Black men of the vote; Plessy (1896) protected these constitutions

items.stem: Mississippi's 1890 constitution and the Southern constitutions that followed it included 'grandfather clauses,' which excused from the new voting requirements any man whose grandfather had been eligible to vote. The effect of these clauses was to
options: (A) restore voting rights to Black men
(B) apply the same voting standard to every citizen
(C) bring the use of poll taxes to an end by replacing them with a simple registration system open to all adult men
(D) protect poor white voters from disfranchisement while poll taxes and literacy tests excluded Black voters
items.explanation: Grandfather clauses were the escape hatch for whites: men whose grandfathers could vote — that is, white men — skipped the poll taxes and literacy tests that were stripping Black men of the vote.

option_explanations.A: Black men's grandfathers had been enslaved and ineligible to vote, so the clause did not help them.
option_explanations.B: The clause created different standards by race, not one standard for all.
option_explanations.C: Poll taxes continued alongside the grandfather clauses.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The clauses shielded white voters from the very requirements that excluded Black voters.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 New South — Mississippi's 1890 constitution: poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses stripped Black men of the vote

items.stem: Historians debate how much the 'New South' really broke from the Old South. The evidence best supports which conclusion?
options: (A) entirely new: the South matched the North in wealth and industry
(B) only partly new: real industry grew, but the labor system echoed slavery's coercion and the region stayed the poorest
(C) not new at all: nothing in the Southern economy changed after the Civil War, with every farm and mill working exactly as in 1860
(D) new only in its politics, while its economy stayed exactly as before
items.explanation: The evidence supports a mixed verdict: Birmingham steel, Piedmont textiles, and Carolina tobacco were real, but industrialization was partial, sharecropping echoed slavery's coercion, and the South remained the nation's poorest region.

option_explanations.A: The wealth gap with the North was not closed; the region stayed the poorest.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Partial industrialization alongside coercive labor and persistent poverty is what the evidence shows.
option_explanations.C: Real industry did grow — Birmingham, the Piedmont mills — so 'nothing changed' is wrong.
option_explanations.D: The economy did change partially; politics changed too, toward legal white supremacy.
